title: How to mark a cross-stitch chart for progress
subtitle: Tracking completed stitches on the chart so you always know where you are
excerpt: Marking a cross-stitch chart as stitches are completed prevents the most common source of miscounts: losing your place when the project is put down. Each completed area is marked on the chart with a pencil, coloured marker, or highlighter so the remaining unmarked areas show exactly what still needs to be stitched.
sourceNotes: Chart progress marking for counted cross-stitch. Standard guidance in major cross-stitch publisher guides.

glossaryTerms.definition: The six-strand embroidery thread used for cross-stitch.

content.text: Marking a chart as you work is a habit that prevents the frustration of losing your place mid-design. A marked chart also lets you see at a glance how much of the design remains and which
colours are still needed. Always mark on a photocopy or print of the chart, never on the original.

Print or photocopy the chart before beginning. A working copy allows you to mark freely without damaging the original, and you can print another copy if the working copy becomes too annotated to read clearly.

Choose a marking method before starting: a pencil X over each completed square is the most common approach. A light-coloured pencil preserves the symbol underneath; a dark pencil or pen makes the mark obvious but obscures the symbol. Coloured highlighter works for black-and-white charts as long as it doesn't obscure the symbol.
Mark each completed square at the end of a row or at the end of a session, not stitch by stitch while working. Marking in batches is faster and does not interrupt the rhythm of stitching.

Verify the marks against the actual stitched piece at the end of each session. Check that every marked square on the chart corresponds to a completed stitch on the fabric. A square marked prematurely — before the stitch was worked — will cause a gap in the design.

Store the marked chart with the project. A chart that is separated from its project may be read by a fresh start: the marks won't be clear without the fabric to reference, and a new session may rework already-completed areas.

items.symptom: The chart marks are too dark to see the original symbol underneath
items.cause: A solid fill or dark pen was used instead of a light X or cross.
items.fix: Use a yellow or light-coloured highlighter for future marking, which tints rather than obscures the square. If the current chart is unreadable, print a fresh copy and re-mark only the areas that need it by comparing carefully against the fabric.

items.symptom: A completed row on the chart doesn't match the stitching on the fabric
items.cause: The marks were added without verifying each stitch was actually done.
items.fix: Compare the marked row on the chart against the fabric stitch by stitch. Any stitch missing on the fabric but marked on the chart needs to be stitched. Unmark any chart square that was marked in error.

content.text: Some stitchers use a magnetic chart keeper with a ruler that slides down the chart row by row, keeping the working row visible while covering the rows above and below. This approach removes the need for a pencil entirely; the magnetic ruler acts as the progress tracker. The method works well for designs with many horizontal rows of the same colour.
